poetry.q: In the practice stanza, which pair of end words tells you that lines 1 and 3 share a rhyme?
options: light / sight
start / sight
pencil / page
poetry.hint: Read the last word of each line aloud. Listen to the vowel and the sounds that follow it.
poetry.why: Light and sight share the same ending sound. Start and heart form the other pair, so the pattern is ABAB.

poetry.q: What does the description “my pencil shivers” suggest about the person holding it?
options: The pencil has been left outdoors.
The writer feels uncertain about starting.
The writer has already filled the page.
poetry.hint: A pencil cannot feel nervous. Look at what the speaker is about to try.
poetry.why: The pencil carries the writer’s nervous movement. That gives us a feeling to compare with the confidence in the final line.

poetry.q: Which explanation makes the strongest case that the crooked star matters?
options: Stars usually have five points.
The star is mentioned near the end.
The first imperfect drawing helps the writer begin.
poetry.hint: Compare the blank page at the beginning with the speaker’s feeling after drawing.
poetry.why: The drawing can symbolize a first attempt. Its effect on the speaker connects a specific image to a message about getting started.

poetry.q: Try a fresh line: “The gate sighed as I started for school.” Which choice identifies the device and its effect?
options: Personification makes the departure feel reluctant.
Rhyme makes every word sound the same.
A simile compares school to a gate using “like”.
poetry.hint: Ask which action normally belongs to a person and consider the mood that action creates.
poetry.why: Giving the gate a sigh lets the setting echo a feeling. The explanation uses both a detail and its effect.

poetry.q: A different stanza ends with “stone / rain / alone / train.” What rhyme scheme do you hear?
options: AABB
ABAB
ABBA
poetry.hint: Assign A to stone, then reuse A only for a matching sound. Do the same for rain.
poetry.why: Stone rhymes with alone and rain rhymes with train. The two pairs alternate.

poetry.q: You wrote “This line uses a metaphor.” Which revision adds analysis?
options: This line has several words.
The author uses many different devices.
Calling a worry a stone suggests that the speaker carries its weight.
poetry.hint: Look for a sentence that explains how the comparison changes the reader’s understanding.
poetry.why: The revised sentence connects a precise comparison to the speaker’s experience. That reasoning helps support a claim.

poetry.q: “I cupped the sound and held it in.” How does the metaphor work?
options: The speaker measures the noise with a tool.
It treats a fading sound like something the speaker can keep.
It tells the exact size of the platform.
poetry.hint: Think about what hands can usually hold and why someone might want to hold a sound.
poetry.why: A sound cannot sit in a palm. The gesture makes the wish to keep hearing it feel physical.

poetry.q: Which words give a reader the strongest clue about sound?
options: “bright as tin”
“crooked star”
“the train hums”
poetry.hint: Try reading with your eyes closed and imagine what you could hear.
poetry.why: “Hums” names a sound. Brightness and shape are visual clues.

poetry.q: Two lines read “The hall was a hive / before the curtain rose.” Which detail best explains the metaphor?
options: People moved and talked busily in the hall.
A beehive was hanging above the stage.
The curtain had six sides.
poetry.hint: What shared quality could connect a crowd waiting for a show to a hive?
poetry.why: The metaphor brings the sound and activity of a hive into the hall, suggesting energy before the show.

poetry.q: A speaker calls an old glove “a small home for my hand.” Which background detail would best support a reading about comfort?
options: A shelf label gives the price.
The speaker puts the glove on when they miss their family.
The glove has five fingers.
poetry.hint: Which detail helps show an emotional connection between this speaker and the object?
poetry.why: Putting on the glove when homesick links an ordinary object with a feeling of belonging.

poetry.q: A poem repeats “wait” in three short lines, then begins the last line with “run.” What is worth investigating?
options: Whether the poem must be describing a race
How many pages the poem needs
How the change from waiting to action shapes the ending
poetry.hint: Read the repeated verb aloud three times, then listen to what happens when it changes.
poetry.why: The repeated word sets a pace and an expectation. The new verb can make the final line feel sudden.

poetry.q: Which caption gives a reader an interpretive reason for a poster design?
options: “I left the top half blank so the tiny star feels like a first step.”
“I filled a sheet of paper.”
“Some words are near the bottom.”
poetry.hint: Look for a choice the artist made and the meaning the viewer might take from it.
poetry.why: The caption connects the space around the star to its meaning. A viewer can look at the page and test that reading.
